# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–23 (Complete – Updated 164)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn of sixth year** (Chapter 23). Rawdon has discovered Rebecca with Steyne and confronted them; has now visited Pitt to make arrangements before likely duel with Steyne. Amelia continues evening vigils at Russell Square. Little Rawdon at school and progressing.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 22 opened "summer of sixth year"; Chapter 23 opens "autumn of sixth year." Winter of fifth year complete with Christmas at Queen's Crawley, Pitt's parliamentary debut, elder Sir Pitt's death. Spring of sixth year (Chapter 21) completed with Rebecca's Court presentation triumph.
- **Locations**: Salwick; Harrowgate; Dunholt; Bryngate; Yarlton; Quenwick; Dunwick; Fenmere; London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Piccadilly, St. James's Street, Russell Square, Baker Street, Hyde Park Ring, Levant House, Foundling Church, Gaunt House, Gaunt Square, Serpentine, Cursitor Street, the Temple, Paddington, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks); Queen's Crawley; Court palace; Gulton; Mirecombe; Brookgreen Fair; Coldcombe; school in City; Astley's; May Fair; Chancery Lane.

## The Catastrophic Discovery and Immediate Aftermath (Chapters 22–23)

**Rawdon's Return Home and Confrontation (Chapter 22–23)**: After Lady Jane's rescue from spunging-house, Rawdon walked home rapidly at nine o'clock. Found drawing-room windows blazing with light. Found Steyne bowing to kiss Rebecca's hand; Rebecca sat in brilliant full toilette, arms sparkling with bracelets and rings, brilliants on breast given by Steyne. Rebecca screamed faintly; Steyne rose grinding teeth, pale with fury.

**Rebecca's Denial and Rawdon's Rage (Chapter 23)**: Rebecca claimed innocence: "I am innocent, Rawdon...before God, I am innocent." Rawdon screamed: "You innocent! Damn you...Every trinket you have on your body is paid for by me. I have given you thousands of pounds, which this fellow has spent and for which he has sold you...You're as innocent as your mother, the ballet-girl, and your husband the bully." **REVELATION**: Rebecca's mother was a ballet-girl; Rawdon's father was a bully.

**Physical Confrontation (Chapter 23)**: Steyne attempted to leave; Rawdon seized Steyne by neckcloth until nearly strangled. Rawdon struck Steyne twice over face with open hand, flung him bleeding to ground. Steyne wore scar to his dying day. Rebecca admired Rawdon: "strong, brave, and victorious."

**Jewel Discovery (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon ordered Rebecca to remove jewels. Rawdon flung open boxes and wardrobes, found desk Amelia had given Rebecca in early days, kept in secret place. **Contents**: Papers, love-letters many years old, trinkets, woman's memoranda, pocket-book with bank-notes. **CRITICAL DISCOVERY**: Bank-notes dated back ten years; one fresh note for **one thousand pounds from Lord Steyne**. **IMPLICATION**: Steyne had been financially supporting Rebecca extensively; this constitutes payment for sexual favors.

**Rebecca's Aftermath (Chapter 23)**: Remained for hours after Rawdon left, sunshine pouring into room. Sat alone on bed's edge; drawers open, contents scattered. Heard him go downstairs, door slamming. **Certainty**: "She knew he would never come back. He was gone forever." **Suicidal ideation**: "Would he kill himself?--she thought--not until after he had met Lord Steyne. She thought of her long past life, and all the dismal incidents of it. Ah, how dreary it seemed, how miserable, lonely and profitless! Should she take laudanum, and end it?" **Recovery attempt**: French maid (her accomplice, in Steyne's pay) persuaded Rebecca to lie down on bed with "entreaty and show of kindness." Maid gathered up trinkets from floor.

## Rawdon's Current Actions (Chapter 23 – Latest Excerpts)

**Morning Appearance at Pitt's Study**: Rawdon arrived at Great Gaunt Street mansion in Great Gaunt Street in his evening costume, which he had worn two days. Appeared blood-shot eyed, hair over face, tumbled clothes. Sat in Pitt's study before his ordered table (blue books, letters, locked account-books, Bible, Quarterly Review, Court Guide). Lady Jane was in nursery superintending children's toilettes and morning prayers (private duty before public ceremonial presided by Pitt).

**Observer Newspaper Discovery**: Valet had read flaming account of "Festivities at Gaunt House" with distinguished personages invited by Marquis of Steyne to meet Royal Highness, before damping and folding paper for Pitt's desk. Account included complimentary though guarded description of Rebecca's famous charades performance. Print fell blank upon Rawdon's eyes; he did not know what he was reading.

**Pitt's Response (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1362)**: Pitt appeared punctually at nine o'clock, fresh, neat, smugly shaved, stiff shirt collar, grey flannel dressing-gown—"a real old English gentleman." Started seeing Rawdon in study in tumbled clothes. Thought Rawdon was not sober, had been out all night on orgy. "Good gracious, Rawdon, what brings you here at this time of the morning? Why ain't you at home?"

**Pitt's Refusal of Financial Help (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1363)**: Pitt cried peevishly: "I always said it would come to this. I warned you a thousand times. I can't help you any more. Every shilling of my money is tied up. Even the hundred pounds that Jane took you last night were promised to my lawyer to-morrow morning. I don't mean to say that I won't assist you ultimately. But as for paying your creditors in full, I might as well hope to pay the National Debt. It is madness. You must come to a compromise."

**Rawdon's Request and Confession (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1364–1365)**: Rawdon spoke in husky voice: "It's the boy. I want you to promise me that you will take charge of him when I'm gone. That dear good wife of yours has always been good to him; and he's fonder of her than he is of his . . .--Damn it. Look here, Pitt--you know that I was to have had Miss Crawley's money. I wasn't brought up like a younger brother, but was always encouraged to be extravagant and kep idle. But for this I might have been quite a different man."

**Revelation of Plan and Suspicion of Duel (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1365)**: Pitt instantly guessed the truth and surmised that Lord Steyne was person whose life Rawdon wished to take. Rawdon told brother briefly in broken accents the circumstances. "It was a regular plan between that scoundrel and her. The bailiffs were put upon me; I was taken as I was going out of his house; when I wrote to her for money, she said she was ill in bed and put me off to another day. And when I got home I found her in diamonds and sitting with that villain alone." Rawdon described personal conflict with Lord Steyne. "To an affair of that nature, there was but one issue, and after his conference with his brother, he was going away to make the necessary arrangements for the meeting which must ensue. And as it may end fatally with me, and as the boy has no mother, I must leave him to you and Jane, Pitt--only it will be a comfort to me if you will promise me to be his friend."

**Financial Settlement (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1366)**: Rawdon took little pocket-book discovered in Becky's desk and drew bundle of notes. "Here's six hundred--you didn't know I was so rich. I want you to give the money to Briggs, who lent it to us--and who was kind to the boy--and I've always felt ashamed of having taken the poor old woman's money. And here's some more--I've only kept back a few pounds--which Becky may as well have, to get on with." As he spoke, hands shook, agitated, pocket-book fell, thousand-pound note fell out.

**Rawdon's Challenge to Steyne (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1367)**: Rawdon hurried from Great Gaunt Street, knocked at bronze Medusa's head on portal of Gaunt House. Purple Silenus porter (red and silver waistcoat) appeared, scared by Colonel's dishevelled appearance, barred way. Rawdon took out card, enjoined porter particularly to send it to Lord Steyne with address written on it: "Colonel Crawley would be all day after one o'clock at the Regent Club in St. James's Street--not at home." Red-faced man looked after him with astonishment as he strode away. People in Sunday clothes joked at cab-stand about his appearance; took carriage, told driver to drive him to Knightsbridge Barracks.

**CRITICAL STATE**: Rawdon has arranged duel with Steyne; prepared for possible death; settled debts with Steyne's own money; entrusted little Rawdon to Pitt and Lady Jane's care; sent challenge to Steyne at Regent Club.

## Key Relationships and Character States

**Rawdon's Transformation and Current Crisis**: Through Lady Jane's kindness and paternal feelings, honest feelings came out. Discovery of Rebecca's affair and financial corruption by Steyne severed marriage permanently. Now arranges duel as matter of honor; moral regeneration evident in decision to pay Briggs and debts using Steyne's money; prepares for possible death; entrusts son to Pitt and Jane.

**Rebecca's Complete Collapse**: From social triumph to utter ruin in single night. Exposed as Steyne's paid mistress. Husband gone forever. Facing scandal and financial destitution. Accomplice maid (in Steyne's pay) her only comfort. Suicidal despair. No path to recovery visible.

**Steyne's Humiliation and Peril**: Exposed as financial corruptor and seducer. Scarred by diamond ornament; wore scar to dying day. Now faces duel with Rawdon; has received challenge at Regent Club.

**Amelia's Continued Anguish**: Separated from son permanently; son indifferent to separation; mother's daily ritual of longing and prayer continues; no resolution in sight. Grows care-worn and sad; sleeps little; weeps and prays in long silent nights.

**Pitt and Lady Jane's Role**: Jane rescued Rawdon from spunging-house; Rawdon overcame with emotion, ran to her, caught her in arms, sobbed on her shoulder. Jane beaming with happiness, prayed humbly for poor way-worn sinner by her own little boy's bed. Now entrusted with care of little Rawdon should Rawdon die in duel. Pitt refuses financial help; money tied up; hundred pounds promised to lawyer tomorrow.

**Little Rawdon at School**: Honest Briggs made up little kit. At school: Young Blackball made him fag, shoe-black, breakfast toaster; initiated him into Latin Grammar; thrashed him three or four times. Rawdon visited and found lad sufficiently well and happy, grinning and laughing in black gown and breeches. Will receive six hundred pounds from Rawdon (Steyne's money) through Pitt.

## Minor Characters
- **Rebecca's mother**: Ballet-girl
- **Rebecca's father (Rawdon's characterization)**: Bully
- **Briggs**: Kind to little Rawdon; will receive six hundred pounds from Rawdon
- **French maid (Finette)**: Rebecca's accomplice, in Steyne's pay
- **Valet to Pitt**: Read newspaper account of Gaunt House festivities before laying it for Pitt
- **Thidrek Corrett**: Packed single trunk, moved from Dunwick to Fenmere
- **Manelle Corrett**: Various minor observations (mispronounced saints, complained of aching back, hummed tune, laughed alone, fell asleep by fire)
